Threat.value: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Memory.value: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing good can happen to me anymore
I feel like an object, not like a person
I was betrayed by someone I trusted

issues.explanation: 'Noticing Weapons' is a poor fit for the stated trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner unless there is evidence of weapon-related assault or generalized violence cues; the rest of the profile centers on interpersonal abuse and nonspecific danger rather than weapon-focused threat monitoring, so this item is hard to reconcile with the trauma context.

'Inaction Guilt' is clinically questionable in this context because it implies self-blame for not doing more to stop the abuse, which is less coherent with an ongoing coercive partner-abuse formulation than appraisals centered on shame, powerlessness, betrayal, or worthlessness. It is not impossible, but paired with the rest of the profile it stands out as weakly aligned with the trauma narrative and node pattern.

vignette: Vinh sat at his desk in the municipal tax office, the fluorescent lights humming overhead as he stared at a discrepancy in a local bakery's ledger. At fifty-one, he had spent decades tracing financial irregularities, but today his attention kept drifting to the corridor behind him. He checked the doorway again, then shifted his chair an inch to the right until his spine rested firmly against the metal filing cabinet. He had come to need that solid pressure; without it, the open-plan office felt dangerously exposed. A stack of invoices slid off a colleague's desk down the hall. Vinh flinched, his pulse spiking as if an intruder had just entered, before he recognized it was only the supply cart. He exhaled, rubbing his temples. The exhaustion settled over him, a familiar heaviness that arrived alongside the same unpredictable shifts in mood he had learned to dread. Three years earlier, a domestic dispute had escalated when his partner's patience snapped. He had been too drained to defend himself, left pinned to the floor as the room spun. The violence had come without warning, shattering his trust and leaving him with the chilling realization that he had been betrayed by the person who knew him best. He could not remember the beginning of the struggle that had brought him here, only sudden pieces of it: the sharp turn of her face, the way his own limbs felt heavy and uncooperative, the sudden impact that erased the moments before. He had tried to hold onto the rest, to find the turning point, but the gaps remained empty, no matter how hard he strained. What frightened him most was that the memory would force its way into his mind during routine audits, unbidden and relentless, until he had to step into the stairwell and press his palms against the cold concrete. He was certain that nothing good could happen to him anymore. The man who used to review accounts with steady hands now felt like a thing being handled, his own thoughts treated as irrelevant while his body was maneuvered against his will. Over the following months, avoidance had woven itself into his daily rhythm. He stopped requesting field audits, telling his supervisor he preferred desk work, though he knew it was because unpredictable schedule changes triggered that same helpless dread. When the office air conditioning kicked on, sending a sharp draft across his neck, he felt a wave of tightness that mirrored the same discomfort he had learned to dread. His wife noticed the distance, the way he flinched when she reached for his shoulder, the nights he lay awake replaying fragments of a fight he could not fully remember. He stopped explaining, stopped trying to make the gaps make sense, carrying the quiet certainty that his days ahead would only hold more disappointment. The weight of it finally pushed him to schedule an intake. He did not know if therapy would help him piece together what was missing or untangle the threads of what remained, but he was tired of living in a state of perpetual alert. He hoped, more than anything, to stop bracing for a blow that no longer came, and to sit in a room without needing to check who might be behind him.
